claims.text: Adding selected lightweight elements to a high-entropy alloy can reduce its overall density.
Selected lightweight-element additions can promote in situ formation of nanoscale ordered intermetallic precipitates.
A precipitation-inducing heat treatment can trigger nucleation of fine ordered phases in the modified alloy.
The nanoscale ordered precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
The ordered phases refine grain boundaries.
The precipitates or ordered phases provide nucleation sites for a robust, stable protective oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
The combined precipitation and oxide-forming effects can increase the alloy's strength-to-weight ratio.
The combined precipitation and oxide-forming effects can improve corrosion resistance.
A stable protective oxide layer can improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have lower density.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit improved corrosion potential and corrosion current density.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will show lower oxidation mass gain during high-temperature exposure.
The performance advantage will persist only within the stability range of the protective oxide layer.
Exceeding the protective oxide layer's stability threshold will cause oxide breakdown and terminate the hypothesized benefits.
Failure to form the required nanoscale precipitate dispersion will eliminate the modified alloy's property advantage over the baseline.
The baseline is initially a homogeneous high-entropy solid solution without engineered lightweight-element-induced nanoscale phase separation.
